name: The Duffy household — a reconstructed labourer (south division)
head: inf_labourer_south_15

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_blk_south_water_franklin_d1_04 is an anonymous reconstructed roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: NO SEPARATE WORKPLACE. A labourer in this town worked in other people's buildings, in the street, or in the dwelling itself, and inventing a shop for the sake of a link would be inventing a building.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: John Duffy

occupation.note: THE LARGEST TRADE IN ANY WESTERN TOWN AND THE ONE NO ROSTER RECORDS, because a labourer advertises nothing, holds no office and joins no church committee - the three ways almost every documented person in this dataset became documented. The harbour works were under construction through 1834 and 1835 (both piers are structure records here), the streets were being graded, and several hundred buildings were being raised. Twelve labouring households are inferred - the largest single group in this layer and still a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies - and every one of them is housed in the meanest roof the schedule carries: a D1 log cabin or a D2 plank shanty. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-14, ON THE SAME TERMS AND FOR THE SAME REASON. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and twelve was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The Randolph and Wells block parcel has since put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division, which is the family this layer houses every one of its eight adopted labourers in and the meanest roof the schedule carries. Thirteen labouring households are inferred. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged; what changed is that a roof exists to hold one more of the households that arithmetic already implied. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-14, ON THE TERMS METHOD RULE 6 SETS AND FOR THE SAME REASON AS THE THIRTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and thirteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at Randolph and Clinton has since put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the WEST Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses nine of its eleven housed labourers in, and the first anonymous roof of that family to stand west of the river. This layer already places two labouring households in the West Division, in raised D2 plank shanties, so the adoption moves no trade across a division line that this programme had not already argued: it houses the fourteenth labourer in a roof the 665-roof programme had already counted instead of raising a fifteenth building. Fourteen labouring households are inferred. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE FOURTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and fourteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at South Water and Franklin has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses ten of its twelve housed labourers in, and a division it already places three labouring households in. Fifteen labouring households are inferred. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged; what changed is that a roof exists to hold one more of the households that arithmetic already implied. BOTH TRADES PASSED ON THIS ONE BLOCK, WHICH IS THE FIRST TIME SINCE THE RULE TOOK ITS THIRD TEST. That is the rule working rather than a quota being filled: the block was dealt a D3 and a D1 by a schedule that knows nothing about this census, and each of the two trades whose committed argument calls its own count a floor is housed in exactly one of those two families in exactly this division. Refusing one of them to keep a parcel to a single adoption would have been a preference dressed as caution. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE FIFTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and fifteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at South Water and Wells has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses eleven of its fifteen labourers in, and a division it already places four labouring households in. Sixteen labouring households are inferred. THE SAME BLOCK OFFERED A SECOND ROOF THIS TRADE PASSES ALL THREE TESTS ON, AND IT WAS REFUSED, for the reason recorded under the carpenters: the block was also dealt a D2 plank shanty, a family this layer houses four labourers in, and the three tests are silent about how many roofs of one block a single trade may take. Both trades were offered a second roof here and both were held to one, which is the conservative reading of a rule that does not say - not a finding that a D2 on this block would have been wrong. ROADMAP K28 records the question. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE SIXTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and sixteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at South Water and LaSalle has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses twelve of its sixteen labourers in, and a division it already places five labouring households in. Seventeen labouring households are inferred. THE SECOND ROOF WAS REFUSED HERE TOO, AND THE REPETITION IS THE FINDING: this block was also dealt a D2 plank shanty, the other family this layer houses labourers in, exactly as South Water and Wells was. Two consecutive blocks have now offered both of this layer's floor trades a second roof apiece, so the case rule 6 does not speak to is not rare - it is what a block of five dwellings in this division looks like when the schedule deals it. Held to one per trade under T-A9's reading, and recorded here as a choice rather than as a rule. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE SEVENTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and seventeen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at South Water and Clark has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses thirteen of its seventeen labourers in, and a division it already places six labouring households in. Eighteen labouring households are inferred. THIS BLOCK DEALT NO D2, WHICH IS THE FIRST TIME SINCE T-A8 THAT THIS TRADE WAS OFFERED ONLY ONE ROOF - so the second-roof question the carpenters met again here did not arise for the labourers, and the one-per-trade reading cost this trade nothing on this block. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE EIGHTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and eighteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at South Water and Dearborn has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses fourteen of its eighteen labourers in, and a division it already places seven labouring households in. Nineteen labouring households are inferred. THE SECOND-ROOF QUESTION RETURNED WITH THE D2 THIS BLOCK WAS DEALT, having skipped one block: T-A11 dealt this trade no D2 at all, and this one does, so the refusal is the same as T-A9's and T-A10's rather than a new argument. Read literally rule 6 admits it - a D2 plank shanty is the other family this layer houses labourers in - and it is refused beside the carpenters' D4 on the same conservative reading. THE ROW CLOSES WITH THE QUESTION OPEN, which is the finding rather than the refusal: of the five blocks of the South Water row, one dealt neither floor trade a second roof, one dealt it to the carpenters alone and three dealt it to both, so the case rule 6 is silent about is what a South Division block of five dwellings ordinarily looks like. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE NINETEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and nineteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at Lake and Market has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses fifteen of its nineteen labourers in, and a division it already places eight labouring households in. Twenty labouring households are inferred. THE SECOND-ROOF QUESTION ARRIVES WITH THE D2 THIS BLOCK WAS DEALT and is refused beside the carpenters' D4 on the same conservative reading, for the sixth time and the first on a block that is not on South Water Street. Read literally rule 6 admits it - a D2 plank shanty is the other family this layer houses labourers in. What the refusal is worth has changed, though: five of the six cases were on one street and could be read as a property of that frontage, and this one cannot, so K28 is settling a question about South Division blocks rather than about the business front. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE TWENTIETH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and twenty was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at Randolph and Franklin has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest dwelling the schedule carries, the family this layer houses sixteen of its twenty labourers in, and a division it already places nine labouring households in. Twenty-one labouring households are inferred. THE D2 THIS BLOCK WAS DEALT IS REFUSED FOR THE SEVENTH TIME AND FOR THE FIRST TIME WITH ITS OTHER CLAIMANT NAMED. Read literally rule 6 admits it - a D2 plank shanty is the other family this layer houses labourers in - and it is refused beside the carpenters' D4 on the same conservative reading. What is new is that the D2 is also the first roof of the LAUNDRESSES, the third of method rule 2's four unbounded trades, housed in D2 and in no other family and already placed in the South Division. So this block's two refused roofs are not two second helpings for two trades; they are four candidacies across four trades, two of which no block parcel has ever named. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE TWENTY-FIRST. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and twenty-one was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at Randolph and Clark has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest dwelling the schedule carries, the family this layer houses seventeen of its twenty-one labourers in, and a division it already places ten labouring households in. Twenty-two labouring households are inferred. THE D2 THIS BLOCK WAS DEALT IS REFUSED FOR THE EIGHTH TIME, AND THIS TIME THE THREE TESTS WERE RUN RATHER THAN RECALLED. tools/measure_adoption_tests.py is committed with this parcel and evaluates rule 6 against the committed text: on a D2 in the South Division exactly one trade passes all three tests, and it is the labourers, taking a second roof on the same conservative reading that has refused it seven times before. WHAT THE COMMAND FOUND THAT NO PARCEL HAD IS THAT T-A14's OTHER TWO CANDIDACIES DO NOT REPRODUCE. T-A14 recorded that the D2 also passes all three tests for the LAUNDRESSES and its D4 for the TEAMSTERS, each being one of method rule 3's four trades argued from the town's building rate rather than from a roof cap. Tests 2 and 3 hold for both. Test 1 does not: rule 6 asks whether the trade's OWN ARGUMENT states in its committed text that its count is a floor, and neither of those two arguments contains any such statement - the only occurrence of the word in the laundress argument is Andreas's 'with the floor covered besides', which is a plank floor in a boarding house. Only the carpenters and the labourers state it, and they have stated it since they were written. So the literal reading of rule 6 admits ONE claimant to this block's D2, not three, and K28's question narrows accordingly: it is no longer 'may a trade that has not asked for a roof be given one' but 'does test 1 mean the trade's own text, or method rule 3's list of unbounded trades'. The two readings disagree for exactly two trades. Nothing here is decided; the refusal stands and the measurement is now a command. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE TWENTY-SECOND, AND AS A BACKFILL RATHER THAN A NEW BLOCK. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and twenty-two was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. blk_randolph_dearborn - which landed before rule 6 had its third test and was never asked the question - has a D1 log cabin standing on lot 3 in the South Division: the meanest dwelling the schedule carries, the family this layer houses eighteen of its twenty-two labourers in, and a division it already places eleven labouring households in. Twenty-three labouring households are inferred. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. THE D2 THIS BLOCK WAS DEALT IS REFUSED FOR THE NINTH TIME, AND THE NINTH REFUSAL IS THE ONE THAT SAYS WHAT THE CANDIDACY WAS MADE OF. Read literally rule 6 admits it, and tools/measure_adoption_tests.py D2 south prints ADOPTABLE for the labourers and for no one else - T-A15's refutation of the laundresses holds here too, on test 1. But the four labouring households this layer houses in a D2 are inf_labourer_shanty_north_a and _b in the NORTH Division and inf_labourer_shanty_west_a and _b in the WEST, and all eleven labourers it houses in the SOUTH Division are in a D1. This layer has never housed a labourer in a D2 in the South Division, so the D2's candidacy - like the carpenters' D4 beside it, and like all sixteen of the anonymous D2 and D4 roofs T-A14 counted in this division - exists only because rule 6 says its three tests are independent. THE STRICTER READING IS NOT OBVIOUSLY RIGHT, AND THE EVIDENCE AGAINST IT IS IN THIS FIELD ALREADY. Requiring the PAIR would refuse the fourteenth labouring household above: T-A4 adopted a D1 in the WEST Division when this layer housed labourers west of the river only in D2 shanties, and argued the adoption in exactly the projected form - the family from one division, the division from another family. Rule 6 names that adoption as one of the four decisions its third test recovers, so a pair reading would break the calibration the rule rests on. That is K28's to settle with both facts in front of it; this parcel measures and refuses to decide.

name_basis.note: THE NAME IS INVENTED. No source names this resident, and this field is not a finding about anybody — it is a label so that a reconstructed household reads as a household rather than as a row in a table. It was drawn from the Irish pool in data/reconstruction/1835_invented_name_pools.json, which is seeded from the names of the 76 ATTESTED residents this project holds — real people, named from cited sources — so that an invented resident is named the way this town's documented residents were actually named rather than the way a story would name one. The community was drawn WITHOUT a weighting that any source supports. An even draw on purpose. The Irish labouring population that later defines this trade in Chicago arrives with the canal contracts of 1836, AFTER the scene date, so weighting 1835 labourers Irish would be importing a later decade into this one. The evidence for the pool itself: Present in the documented layer but thinly: one attested resident's origin is given as 'County Kerry, Ireland, by way of Lancashire, Dublin, Quebec, Montreal, New York, Virginia and Newark', and the attested surnames Egan and Casey belong to this stock. THE WEIGHTING TOWARD LABOURING TRADES IS ITSELF AN INFERENCE and is marked as such wherever it is applied: the Illinois and Michigan Canal contracts were not let until 1836, so the large Irish labouring population of the later 1830s is arriving around and after the scene date rather than established by it. What the pool claims is that Irish names belong in this town on 1 July 1835, which the documented layer supports; it does not claim any particular trade was Irish.
